newsitem.title: USA: Hispanics ask Clinton to help Central Americans.
newsitem.headline: Hispanics ask Clinton to help Central Americans.

text.p: A group of Hispanic congressmen on Wednesday called on President Bill Clinton to fulfil his pledge to help hundreds of thousands of Central American immigrants facing deportation from the United States.

Members of the Hispanic caucus said Clinton must keep a promise he made this month to Central American presidents in Costa Rica that the United States would not permit large scale expulsions under its new laws against illegal immigration.

"Unless President Clinton, or Congress, take action immediately, a quarter of a million people may be deported ... and lose everything they have spent a decade building," Representative Luis Gutierrez, an Illinois Democrat, told a news conference.

The congressmen said some 240,000 Salvadoreans, Guatemalans and Nicaraguans who came to the United States during the 1980s fleeing from civil wars now risked being sent back to their impoverished countries.
Salvadoreans and Guatemalans were protected from deportation under a 1990 settlement of a class action suit against the Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS).
Thousands of Nicaraguans, on the other hand, were allowed to remain in the United States during the past decade while their country was ruled by the leftist Sandinistas.
According to the Hispanic congressmen, the immigration law passed last year changed the rules for Central Americans seeking to become permanent U.S. residents.
Provisions of the legislation that came into effect in April set tougher conditions for foreigners seeking to avoid deportation and established a quota of 4,000 exceptions a year.
The INS, which has seen its budget more than double under Clinton, hopes to expell at least 93,000 illegal immigrants this year, up from some 68,000 last year.

The Hispanic congressmen want Clinton to take immediate administrative action to 'grandfather in' the Salvadoreans and Guatemalans and all eligible Nicaraguans so the INS may review their cases under the laws in force when they arrived here.
If the White House does not move in that direction, Gutierrez said the Hispanic caucus stood ready to introduce legislation to that same effect.
Democratic whip Bob Menendez, a New Jersey representative of Cuban origin, said the new immigration law sent the wrong message abroad about the United States' goals.

"You cannot go to Central America and tell their presidents that you do not intend to have massive deportations of Central Americans and then come home and do virtually nothing. And that is in essence what's happening," he said.
